notes.meaning: Moses answers God with worry. He fears the Israelites will not believe him or listen to his words. After four hundred years without an appearance from God, Moses worries the people will say the Lord never spoke to him at all.

The Lord asks Moses what is in his hand, and Moses answers that it is a staff. This was his ordinary wooden shepherd's stick, used for walking and guiding sheep. God was about to use this everyday tool to display His mighty power.

God tells Moses to throw the staff to the ground, and it turns into a living snake. Moses is so startled and frightened that he runs away from it. This showed that God has authority over dangerous creatures and over the serpent symbols of Egypt.

The Lord commands Moses to reach out and catch the snake by the tail. Moses overcomes his fear, takes hold of it, and it turns back into a wooden staff in his hand. It takes great faith to obey God when something seems dangerous, but God keeps His promises to protect His servants.

God explains that this miracle is given so the people will believe Moses. It will prove to Israel that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has truly appeared to him. Miracles served as clear signs that a messenger was sent directly by God.

The Lord gives Moses a second sign by telling him to put his hand inside his cloak. When Moses pulls it out, his skin is covered with a severe, white disease known as leprosy. God showed that He can strike the human body with disease in an instant.

God commands Moses to place his hand back inside his cloak, and when he takes it out, it is completely healed. His skin is fresh and healthy again, just like the rest of his body. This proved that God not only brings judgment, but also has the power to heal and restore.

The Lord explains that if the people do not believe the first sign of the staff, the second sign of the healed hand may convince them. God's miracles speak like a voice to the conscience. God is patient and provides enough evidence to help people put their trust in Him.

God gives a third sign in case the people still doubt Moses after the first two. Moses is told to pour water from the Nile River onto dry ground, where it will instantly turn into blood. The Egyptians treated the Nile as a god of life, so this sign proved that the Lord was far greater and would bring judgment on Egypt.

Moses raises another excuse, saying he has never been a good speaker and is slow of speech. He feels that having a clumsy tongue makes him unfit to speak to kings or lead a nation. Even when God calls us, we often look at our own weaknesses instead of trusting God's strength.

The Lord answers Moses by asking who made the human mouth and who decides whether a person can see, hear, or speak. Since God formed all human senses, He has the power to overcome any flaw or weakness. We can trust the Creator to give us what we need to carry out His commands.

God gives a direct order for Moses to go, promising to be with his mouth and teach him what to say. Moses would not have to rely on his own cleverness because God would guide his speech. When the Lord sends someone on an errand, He always provides the help they need.

Moses still shrinks back from the assignment and pleads with God to send anyone else. He has run out of arguments and simply does not want to go. Fear of failure can make us want to step aside even when God has promised His help.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Many early church fathers and older Catholic commentators understood Moses to be asking God to send the promised Messiah instead.

notes.meaning: The Lord becomes angry because Moses stubbornly resists His call, but He still shows mercy by providing Aaron as a helper. Aaron the Levite is already on his way and will be glad to see his brother. God knew that Aaron was a skilled speaker who could assist in the work.

God instructs Moses to speak to Aaron and give him the words to say. The Lord promises to help both brothers speak and to guide them in everything they must do. God works through different people by giving each one a role to play.

Aaron will serve as the spokesman to the people, acting like a mouth for Moses. Moses will stand in the place of God to Aaron by passing along the Lord's instructions. God set up a clear order so that His message would be spoken faithfully.

God tells Moses to take the shepherd's staff with him so he can perform miraculous signs with it. The simple wooden stick in his hand would become a sign of divine authority. God delights in using humble tools to do wonderful works.

Moses returns to his father-in-law Jethro and asks for permission to travel back to his relatives in Egypt to see if they are alive. Jethro gives his blessing, telling Moses to go in peace. Moses acted with kindness and respect toward his family before setting out on his journey.

While Moses is still in Midian, the Lord speaks to him again and tells him to go back to Egypt right away. God reassures him that the men who wanted to take his life are all dead. God removes obstacles and eases our fears as we step out in obedience.

Moses puts his wife and sons on a donkey and begins the journey back toward Egypt, holding the staff of God in his hand. The shepherd's staff is now called the staff of God because God's power will work through it. Moses moved forward with his whole family, ready to do what God commanded.

God tells Moses to perform all the wonders He has commanded before Pharaoh, but warns that He will harden Pharaoh's heart so he will refuse to let the people go. God revealed this ahead of time so Moses would not be discouraged when the king resisted. Even the stubbornness of rulers cannot stop God's great plan of rescue.

differ.view: God sovereignly hardens Pharaoh's heart according to His own purpose and holy judgment, demonstrating His absolute rule over human hearts.
Pharaoh first hardened his own heart against God's light, and God then permitted his heart to become fully hardened as a consequence of his choice.

notes.meaning: Moses is instructed to tell Pharaoh that Israel is the Lord's firstborn son. This showed that God loved Israel deeply and chose them as His special covenant people. God defends His children just as a father protects his own family.

God demands that Pharaoh let His son go so that Israel can worship Him, and warns that if Pharaoh refuses, God will kill Pharaoh's firstborn son. This severe warning looked forward to the final plague that would strike Egypt. God holds oppressors accountable for the way they treat His people.

At an overnight lodging place on the road, the Lord meets Moses and seeks to put him to death. Moses had neglected to circumcise his son, failing to obey God's covenant sign in his own home. Before Moses could lead the people of God, he had to be faithful to God's commands in his own family.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often see this passage as an ancient account using picturesque language to describe Moses suddenly falling dangerously sick.

notes.meaning: Zipporah takes a sharp flint knife, cuts off her son's foreskin, and touches it to Moses' feet. She calls Moses a bridegroom of blood because of the ceremony that saved his life. Her prompt action showed that obedience to God's covenant is necessary and urgent.

differ.view: Zipporah held up the blood to remind God of His promise. This points to Jesus, the true "Bridegroom of Blood," who stands between us and God's anger. Baptism has now taken the place of circumcision.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some suggest "bridegroom of blood" was once an old saying tied to circumcision before marriage.

notes.meaning: The Lord spares Moses and lets him recover once the circumcision is carried out. Zipporah used the phrase bridegroom of blood to refer to the covenant act that had just taken place. When God's people correct their mistakes, God responds with mercy.

Meanwhile, the Lord tells Aaron to go into the wilderness to meet Moses. Aaron travels to the mountain of God, meets his brother, and kisses him in joyful greeting. God was faithful to bring the brothers together after forty long years apart.

Moses shares with Aaron all the words the Lord had sent him to speak and all the signs he was commanded to perform. The two brothers talked openly so they could work together with one mind. Sharing God's message clearly helps leaders serve the Lord as a team.

Moses and Aaron arrive in Egypt and gather all the elders of the Israelites together. They met with the family leaders and tribal heads to present God's plan. God works in an orderly way by reaching out to the leaders of His people first.

Aaron tells the leaders everything the Lord had revealed to Moses, and Moses performs the miraculous signs in the sight of the people. Aaron faithfully served as the speaker just as God had planned. The wonders confirmed that the message came straight from heaven.

The people of Israel believe the report, and when they hear that the Lord has seen their suffering and cares for them, they bow their heads in worship. After centuries of slavery, their hearts are filled with gratitude and trust toward God. Remembering God's care moves us to worship Him with thankful hearts.
